<reason>A wins the decisive clash. B built a clever conditional frame ("harm in one implementation, help in every one") and extracted a real concession via Q1 (near-zero harm where hours hold), but A neutralized it with the strongest analytic move of the debate: time-cutting is not an independent confound but the very mechanism by which four-day weeks save money ("harm and savings are the same dial"). A's fork in A4.5 forced B to win retention in every branch, and retention was B's weakest plank — under direct pressure (A's Q2) B conceded turnover comparisons are "noisy" and leaned on unmeasured applicant-pool reports, letting A land "an unmeasured benefit cannot outweigh a measured harm." B's escape in B4.5 required stretching A's "small or near zero" concession from time-holders to all adopters, a misattribution A cleanly exposed in A5.3. B's "retention is itself learning" reframe was genuinely original and rhetorically excellent, but it was answered on measurement grounds and never quantified, while A's "as adopted, not as imagined" framing better fit the comparative motion. Both sides showed strong epistemic discipline (no fake citations, honest approximations) and memorable rhetoric; clipping costs were roughly symmetric and non-decisive.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2 (A4.1/A4.5): the endogeneity point that savings and harm move together, crystallized into the both-ways fork — either most districts hold hours (savings shrink, retention left to carry the motion unmeasured) or most cut time (B has conceded the learning loss). B never escaped it without misattributing A's concession, which A punished in the closing.</best_rebuttal>
